title: Postal codes narrow the region
description: German postal codes have five digits and the first two place you in a region. They turn up on shop fronts, vans and address plates.

title: Phone codes narrow the region
description: German landline numbers are written (xxxx) xxx xx xxx and the first two or three digits place you in a region. Numbers starting 01xx are mobile and carry no location.

title: Metal frame above the insulators
description: A concrete pole with a thin split bar at the top whose insulators stand up above the bar rather than hanging below it. The giveaway is the small metal construction sitting above the insulators. Bavaria and Baden-Württemberg.

title: Pole top wrapped in duct tape
description: A concrete pole with a thin split bar and the insulators standing up, with what looks like duct tape wrapped around the top. Limited to three states.

title: Insulators neither up nor down
description: A concrete pole with a split bar at the top whose insulators sit level with the bar, neither standing above it nor hanging below.

title: Very thin split bar
description: A concrete pole whose split bar is thinner than usual and attached differently, with the insulators hanging down. A near-identical variant exists with a slightly wider bar attached the normal way, so it is easy to miss — but a very thin bar points to Bavaria.

title: Thin split bar attached normally
description: Close to the very thin variant but with a slightly thicker bar, attached the ordinary way. Possibly most common in Mecklenburg-Vorpommern.

title: Pole top with red duct tape
description: A variant whose insulators look longer and sit further out towards the ends of the bar, with red duct tape at the top. The difference from the plain thin-bar pole is subtle and best learnt by comparing the two.

title: Right-left-right bar
description: A pole top whose insulators alternate right, left, right along the bar and hang downwards. Eastern Lower Saxony and Saxony-Anhalt, and also Mecklenburg-Vorpommern.

title: Serbian-looking metal pole
description: A metal lattice construction in place of a concrete or wooden pole, resembling the ones used in Serbia.

title: Cap on top of a wooden pole
description: A separate piece fitted over the top of a wooden pole. It also occurs in Norway, Sweden, Finland and Estonia. When the piece is flat rather than pointed it appears to mean Bavaria.

title: Hook pole
description: A pole top shaped like a hook. Not exclusive to Germany — Latvia among others has it too.

title: North Rhine-Westphalia and Hesse have only round wooden poles
description: These two states use round wooden poles almost exclusively, with round concrete poles turning up only rarely. Any other pole type argues against them.

title: Blue car with an antenna
description: One of the four German cars. The antenna argues against going north, though it is not impossible there.

title: No car, no antenna
description: Coverage showing neither car nor antenna. Far less common than the two blue cars, and concentrated in a group of states.

title: Bollard bolted to the guardrail
description: Germany fixes its bollards straight onto the guardrail far more often than any neighbouring country. Others do it, but nowhere near as systematically.

title: Bollard with a blue reflector
description: A bollard whose reflector is blue rather than white or grey. Exclusive to Lower Saxony, and easy to confuse with a grey reflector.

title: Yellow plate above the reflector
description: A small yellow plate fixed above the bollard's reflector. Essentially exclusive to Lower Saxony. Other colours occur, white and green excepted, but more rarely.

title: Black triangular sticker on bollards
description: A black triangular sticker carrying a crescent-like shape, stuck on the bollard. Very common across the country.

title: Blue and white reflector beside the bollard
description: A separate small reflector, blue and white, planted next to the bollard. Uncommon, but most often seen in Bavaria.

title: Round reflector on the guardrail
description: A round reflector set into the guardrail itself. Most common in Mecklenburg-Vorpommern and Bavaria but possible in every state, and no other country does this.

title: Guardrail ending in a loop
description: The guardrail curls back on itself in a closed loop at its end. Very common and very helpful in two northeastern states.

title: Signs bolted top and bottom
description: German sign posts are bolted with two fixings at the top of the sign and two at the bottom. Only Iceland, Denmark, Hungary and Greece attach theirs in a similar way.

title: Black top on the sign back
description: The back of the sign carries a black strip along its top edge. Common, and shared only with Czechia, Luxembourg and Poland; Slovakia sometimes has a similar top.

title: Flat sign backs, not folded
description: German sign backs are often completely flat, whereas Luxembourg folds the edges on every one of its signs. Folded edges do occur in Germany too, so the test only works one way.

title: White sticker on almost every sign
description: A small white sticker is stuck on nearly every road sign in Germany. It varies in size and detail but its presence is near universal.

title: Red and white chevrons only
description: German chevron boards are red and white. Red and yellow ones exist but are very rare.

title: White sign with a thin double border
description: A white sign carrying a small black border with a small white border outside it. Very common in Germany and Czechia; Slovakia's version has a noticeably thinner white border.

title: Marker with a triangular cap
description: A roadside marker topped by a small triangular cap above the number plate. The author is unsure how far beyond the highlighted states it goes.

title: Saarland's two-part white sign
description: A white sign split into two horizontal sections reading L followed by one to three digits, the number of the minor road. By far most common in Saarland.

title: Yellow marker with a yellow cap
description: A yellow post topped by a wide yellow cap, seen in four states. A very similar post without the cap is found everywhere and is no help.

title: Road letters give away the state
description: Saxony has no L roads at all and is the only state using S roads, which appear on signs but not on the map. Bavaria is the only state using St roads, which appear on both. Thuringia and Hesse have only four-digit L roads, never three-digit ones.

title: White-red-white painted posts
description: Posts painted in white, red and white bands. As far as the author could tell this exact sequence means Nuremberg, Münster or Dortmund; other sequences such as white-red-white-red-white occur elsewhere in Germany.

title: White and blue stickers side by side
description: A white sticker with a slightly smaller blue one beside it — beside, not above or below. Specific to Lower Saxony.

title: Blue and white stripes around the sign post
description: A sign post wrapped in blue and white stripes. Exclusive to North Rhine-Westphalia.

title: Orange and black striped post
description: A slim post banded in orange and black. Czechia and Slovakia use taller versions showing more bands, typically two orange and two black.

title: White version of the striped post
description: The same post in a white version rather than the usual colours. Specific to North Rhine-Westphalia.

title: Red above the yellow marker
description: A yellow roadside marker with a red section at the top. The plain yellow marker on its own is found everywhere and means nothing.

title: Blue version of the yellow marker
description: A blue version of the same roadside marker, which appears to be unique to a small group of states.

title: Yellow bands on Bielefeld traffic lights
description: Bielefeld wraps yellow bands around its traffic light poles right across the city. Look around and you can often spot several at once.

title: Spanish-flag band on sign posts
description: A red-yellow-red band, the colours of the Spanish flag, wrapped around sign posts of various kinds, not only bus stop signs. By far most common in Bavaria, with some reported in Lower Saxony.

title: Green traffic lights
description: Traffic light housings painted green rather than the usual dark grey or black.

title: Dortmund and Essen traffic light
description: A traffic light of a design found only in Dortmund and Essen. A similar-looking one exists everywhere, so the difference is worth learning.

title: Brown wheelie bin
description: Wheelie bins of this particular brown style, with a brown lid on a brown body.

title: Green wheelie bin
description: Wheelie bins of this particular green style.

title: Dutch houses in Germany
description: Red brick houses with panelled roofs, Dutch-style pavement and a flat landscape — effectively the Netherlands on the German side of the border. By far most common in western Lower Saxony. Western North Rhine-Westphalia looks similar and is easy to confuse with it.

title: Polish houses in Germany
description: Houses that look like Poland's, in flat to gently hilly country.

title: Very colourful concrete houses
description: Streets of concrete houses rendered in strong, varied colours.

title: Sharp roofs and white buildings
description: Very sharply pitched roofs, often on very white buildings, reminiscent of northern Austria. Mountains are usually visible nearby, generally to the south.

title: Grapevines on orange brick houses
description: Orange to brownish brick found west of Mannheim towards the French border. The grapevines trained up the house fronts, and the window shapes, mark the area just as well.

title: Bavarian church tower
description: Bavarian church towers have a distinctive rounded, onion-shaped top. They occur in Baden-Württemberg too but rarely.

title: Black Forest farmhouse
description: Houses with very low, broad roofs and long balconies, mostly in the rural central and southern Black Forest.

title: Hamburg's wide construction road
description: A very wide road carrying a great deal of yellow construction marking, running right through Hamburg along the A7. An unpaved new road under construction is often visible to the east, and windmills to the west, or you find yourself inside a harbour.

title: Stuttgart tram rails
description: Roads throughout Stuttgart carry this style of tram rail set into the middle of the carriageway.

title: Horizontal leaf smudge west of Münster
description: A few L roads around the town of Billerbeck, west of Münster, carry a horizontal leaf smudge on the camera.

title: Orange stripe on wind turbines
description: Wind turbines are found all over Germany rather than only near the coast, and the orange or red stripe painted around the tower may well be unique to the country.

title: Orange fire hydrant markers
description: German fire hydrant markers are mostly orange or red. The author reports a noticeably higher density of them in Bavaria, and a grey version found only there.

title: Power lines running onto roofs
description: Power lines attached directly to house roofs occur in Rhineland-Palatinate, Saarland, Baden-Württemberg and southern Bavaria, and rarely in North Rhine-Westphalia.

title: Roof tiles used as wall cladding
description: Houses clad with ordinary clay roof tiles on their walls, often the whole gable or facade. Found roughly between Hanover, Magdeburg and Kassel. Don't confuse with a steep roof coming down low, slate-like shingles or mansard roofs: here the tiles hang on a vertical wall.

title: Beaver-tail tile wall cladding
description: Wall cladding made of beaver-tail tiles (flat tiles with a rounded lower edge, laid in overlapping rows). Within the tile-cladding area, most common between Hanover and Kassel.

title: Flat tile wall cladding
description: Wall cladding made of flat roof tiles with sharp vertical edges. Within the tile-cladding area, most common between Hanover and Magdeburg.

title: Hollow tile wall cladding
description: Wall cladding made of hollow (pantile) roof tiles: wave-shaped, without sharp vertical edges, which tells them apart from flat tiles. Within the tile-cladding area, mostly found in the west, between Hanover and Göttingen.

title: Reform tile wall cladding
description: Wall cladding made of reform tiles (a variant of interlocking tile). Within the tile-cladding area, most common west of Kassel, less around Hanover.

title: Brim tile wall cladding
description: Wall cladding made of brim tiles (flat tiles with a thick lip along their lower edge, giving strong horizontal lines). Within the tile-cladding area, most common in the east, between Hanover and Magdeburg.

title: Arched brick panels east of Minden
description: Brick wall cladding with odd arched panels, always with a semicircular surface at the bottom. Very specifically found east of Minden, north of Bad Oeynhausen, and seemingly unique to that area.

title: Red brick farmyards with green gates
description: Huge farmhouses combining bright red bricks, bright red roof tiles and green gates and shutters. Typical of the area northwest of Hanover up to Bremen, plus a pocket around Lüneburg. Sheet metal barn roofs are rare there.

title: Sheet metal barn roofs in northern Lower Saxony
description: Farm barns with corrugated sheet metal roofs. In the red-brick farm country of Lower Saxony they are most common in the north: between Bremerhaven, Stade and Hamburg, and towards Lübeck and Lüneburg. Rare northwest of Hanover.

title: German pole tops
description: Four useful pole tops: the trident, fairly useful for the south; the triangle, usually in the west but not fully reliable; the thick crossbar, reminiscent of Argentine poles, a very good clue for the north-east; and the rounded crossbar, found only in south-eastern Bavaria (the rest of Bavaria has a small cap on the middle bar instead).

title: Plates on trees (Mecklenburg and Brandenburg)
description: These green-and-white (sometimes black-and-white) plates fixed on roadside trees are unique to Mecklenburg-Vorpommern and Brandenburg.
